title: Why Adonijah Tried to Take the Throne Before David Died
paragraphs: Why Adonijah Tried to Take the Throne Before David Died
There are moments in Scripture that feel disturbingly modern.

A father grows weak. A family fractures quietly behind palace walls. Ambition disguises itself as destiny. People smile publicly while secretly calculating power. A kingdom waits nervously for what comes next.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it… a son decides he is tired of waiting.
That son was Adonijah.

Most believers know David. Many know Solomon. But few truly understand the terrifying emotional, political, spiritual, and prophetic storm that exploded in the shadows before Solomon ever touched the throne.
Because Adonijah’s rebellion was not merely a political coup.
It was a collision between flesh and prophecy. Human ambition against divine appointment. Appearance against obedience. Charisma against covenant.
And if we are honest… many people reading this are fighting the exact same battle inside themselves.
Not for a literal throne.
But for control. Recognition. Validation. Position. Influence. The need to force what God never told them to take.
That is why this story still burns.
Because Adonijah did not look evil.
He looked qualified.
And sometimes the most dangerous people are not the obviously wicked ones. Sometimes they are the beautiful, gifted, persuasive people who were never actually chosen by God for the role they crave.
The story begins in 1 Kings 1.
David is old. Weak. Fragile. Scripture says:
“Now king David was old and stricken in years; and they covered him with clothes, but he gat no heat.” (1 Kings 1:1)
The Hebrew phrase translated “stricken in years” carries the idea of being advanced, entered deeply into days, exhausted by age.
The Hebrew reads:
זָקֵן בָּא בַּיָּמִים
“Zaqen ba bayyamim”
Literally: “Old, entering into days.”
David—the giant killer. The warrior king. The worshipper. The fugitive. The man after God’s own heart.
Now shivering under blankets.
And kingdoms become vulnerable when strong men grow weak.
People begin positioning themselves.
This is where Adonijah enters.
Scripture says:
“Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king.” (1 Kings 1:5)
That sentence is one of the most chilling lines in the entire Old Testament.
Because Scripture does not say:
“God called Adonijah.” “God anointed Adonijah.” “God chose Adonijah.”
It says:
“He exalted himself.”
The Hebrew phrase is:
וַיִּתְנַשֵּׂא אֲדֹנִיָּה
“Vayyitnasse Adoniyah”
The root word carries the idea of lifting oneself up, elevating oneself, exalting oneself.
This was self-promotion. Self-coronation. Self-enthronement.
And that spirit still exists today.

People appoint themselves into ministries God never called them to. People chase platforms before prayer. People crave visibility more than holiness. People want crowns without crushing. People want influence without obedience.
Adonijah did not wait for God.
He announced himself.
“I will be king.”
Not: “If the Lord wills.” Not: “If the prophet confirms.” Not: “If my father decrees.”
Just: “I will.”
That is the language of flesh.
And yet… if we are being honest… Adonijah looked like the obvious choice.
He was David’s son. He was handsome. He had royal blood. He had influence. He had powerful supporters.
Scripture even pauses to describe his appearance.
“He also was a very goodly man.” (1 Kings 1:6)
The Hebrew says:
טוֹב תֹּאַר מְאֹד
“Tov to’ar me’od”
Very beautiful in form.
Adonijah had optics. Presence. Image.
And humanity has always confused appearance with anointing.
But God has never been hypnotized by outward beauty.
Israel once did the exact same thing with Saul. Tall. Impressive. Kingly-looking.
Yet heaven had already chosen differently.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.

Because many people secretly believe that if they look prepared enough, sound confident enough, gather enough support, or create enough momentum… God will eventually endorse what He never actually ordained.
But heaven is not manipulated by branding.
Adonijah gathered chariots. Horsemen. Fifty men to run before him.
It was political theater. A manufactured image of inevitability.
He wanted people to feel: “This must be the next king.”
But crowds cannot create calling.
Only God can.
And then Scripture quietly reveals one of the deepest parental failures in David’s life.
“His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?” (1 Kings 1:6)
David corrected nations. But failed to correct his son.
That line hits harder the older you get.
Because love without correction can become destruction disguised as kindness.
The Hebrew thought behind this passage suggests David never crossed or restrained him. Never challenged him. Never confronted him.
Adonijah grew up unchecked.
And unchecked pride eventually demands a throne.
Many modern believers want authority but reject correction.
The moment someone rebukes them, they leave. The moment accountability appears, they disappear. The moment leadership wounds their ego, they call it persecution.
But uncorrected ambition becomes spiritually lethal.
Adonijah then begins gathering allies.
Joab joins him. Abiathar the priest joins him.
This is what makes rebellion dangerous.
It rarely looks isolated.
It often attracts respected people.
And this shocks many believers.
“How could spiritual people support something God never chose?”
Because proximity to sacred things does not always mean surrender to God.
Even priests can become politically compromised. Even experienced leaders can mistake momentum for anointing.
Adonijah then hosts a sacrificial feast.
Notice the deception.
He wraps rebellion in religious imagery.
That still happens today.
Not everything done “in God’s name” is actually approved by God.
Some people use spiritual language to baptize ambition.
And then one of the most revealing details appears.
Adonijah intentionally did NOT invite Solomon.
He excluded the one heaven had chosen.
Because flesh recognizes threats.
Deep down, Adonijah knew.
He knew Solomon existed. He knew David had spoken. He knew prophecy was circulating.
But ambition has a terrifying ability to silence inconvenient truth.
And this is where Bathsheba enters the story.
The same Bathsheba many people reduce only to scandal.
Yet here she becomes part of preserving the covenant line that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ.
Nathan the prophet approaches her.
Notice this carefully.
God responds to Adonijah’s self-exaltation through prophetic intervention.
Nathan asks Bathsheba:
“Hast thou not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith doth reign, and David our lord knoweth it not?” (1 Kings 1:11)
The kingdom is being stolen while David is still alive.
And spiritually, this reveals something terrifying.
Things can seize territory in your life while your discernment sleeps.
People can slowly enthrone pride. Sin. Bitterness. Compromise. Lust. Control. Self-worship.
Until eventually the false king is sitting where only God belongs.
Bathsheba reminds David of his promise concerning Solomon.
Then Nathan confirms it.
And suddenly the atmosphere shifts.
David rises.
Weak body. Strong covenant.
And this matters deeply.
Because even in David’s failures, the covenant promise of God still moved forward.
God had already chosen Solomon.
Not because Solomon was flawless. Not because Bathsheba’s story was clean. Not because David deserved it.
But because God’s purposes are built on grace.
David commands:
“Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule.” (1 Kings 1:33)
The mule symbolized royal authority.
Then Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint Solomon.
The Hebrew concept of anointing here carries the sacred separation for divine purpose.
Oil was not cosmetic.
It symbolized heaven’s selection.
And suddenly the city erupts:
“God save king Solomon.”
The Hebrew phrase:
יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹה
“Yechi hamelech Shelomoh”
“May King Solomon live.”
The sound shakes the earth.
And Adonijah hears it.
Can you imagine that moment?
The panic. The realization. The collapse of self-made destiny.
One moment he thinks he is becoming king. The next moment heaven publicly exposes that he was never chosen.
This is one of the hardest truths many people will ever face:
Not every open door is God. Not every opportunity is divine. Not every applause is confirmation. Not every platform is anointing.
Sometimes God allows people to reveal their hearts publicly before judgment arrives.
Adonijah runs to the altar and grabs the horns seeking mercy.
And here the story becomes astonishing.
Solomon shows restraint. Mercy.
“If he will shew himself a worthy man, there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth.” (1 Kings 1:52)
Mercy was available.
But Adonijah’s heart was never truly surrendered.
Later, he attempts another political maneuver involving Abishag.
To modern readers this may seem strange.
But in ancient Near Eastern royal culture, taking a former king’s concubine could symbolize claiming royal authority.
Solomon immediately recognizes the deeper meaning.
Adonijah was still trying to grasp the throne.
He had not repented. He had merely paused.
That distinction matters eternally.
Many people stop behavior temporarily without truly surrendering their heart.
Fear interrupted Adonijah. But fear did not transform him.
And eventually judgment fell.
This story is not merely about ancient palace politics.
It is about the human condition.
It is about what happens when ambition outruns obedience.
It is about the terrifying danger of trying to seize what God has not given.
It is about the difference between self-exaltation and divine appointment.
Jesus Himself later taught this principle.
In Luke 14:11, the Greek says:
ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται
“Hoti pas ho hypson heauton tapeinothesetai”
“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.”
Notice the connection.
Adonijah exalted himself.
And eventually he was brought low.
But the Gospel reveals something even deeper.
Humanity itself has an Adonijah problem.
Since Eden, mankind has tried to enthrone itself.
“I will.” “My way.” “My truth.” “My desires.” “My kingdom.”
Sin at its core is attempted self-rule.
But Jesus Christ came as the true King.
Not self-exalted. Not grasping. Not manipulating.
Philippians 2 reveals the opposite spirit.
The Greek says Christ:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
“Heauton ekenosen”
“He emptied Himself.”
Adonijah exalted himself. Jesus emptied Himself.
Adonijah grasped for a throne. Jesus carried a cross.
Adonijah used appearance. Jesus was “despised and rejected of men.”
Adonijah gathered political supporters. Jesus washed feet.
And yet Jesus alone is the rightful King.
This is why the Gospel transforms everything.
Because Christ does not merely expose false kings. He replaces them.
The throne inside the human heart was never meant for ego. Pride. Lust. Ambition. Control. Addiction. Bitterness. Self-worship.
It belongs to Jesus.
Some people reading this are exhausted because they have spent years trying to force doors open God never intended.
Trying to become what looks impressive instead of becoming obedient.
Trying to manufacture significance.
Trying to prove worth.
Trying to sit on thrones that were destroying their soul.
But there is freedom in surrender.
Because what God truly ordains never requires fleshly striving to sustain it.
Be honest. This hit harder than some expected.
Someone is secretly exhausted from trying to become king over a life they were never designed to rule.
Some people lose their soul chasing crowns they were never called to wear.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Sinubukan ni Adonijah na Kunin ang Trono Bago Mamatay si David
May mga kuwento sa Biblia na parang sobrang layo sa modernong panahon.
Pero may mga kuwento rin na parang salamin.
At kapag binasa mo sila nang mabuti… parang ikaw ang nakikita mo.
Ito ang isa sa mga iyon.
Isang matandang hari na unti-unti nang nanghihina. Isang pamilya na tahimik nang nababasag. Mga taong nagkukunwaring loyal pero may sariling agenda. Isang anak na hindi na kayang maghintay.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon… may isang lalaking nagsabi:
“Ako na ang magiging hari.”
Hindi ito simpleng political drama.
Ito ay kwento ng pride. Ambisyon. Pagmamadali. Pag-agaw sa bagay na hindi pa ibinibigay ng Diyos.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao ngayon ang may parehong laban.
Hindi man literal na trono.
Pero kontrol. Pagkilala. Posisyon. Impluwensya. Kapangyarihan. Validation.
At minsan, kahit Kristiyano na tayo… may bahagi pa rin ng puso natin na gustong pilitin ang timing ng Diyos.
Doon nagsisimula ang kwento ni Adonijah.
Sa 1 Hari 1, matanda na si David.
Ang dating mandirigmang hari… nanginginig na sa lamig.
Sabi ng Kasulatan:
“Now king David was old and stricken in years...” (1 Kings 1:1)
Sa Hebrew:
זָקֵן בָּא בַּיָּמִים
“Zaqen ba bayyamim”
Ibig sabihin: “Matanda na, malalim na ang pinasok na mga araw.”
Napakaganda ng larawan.
Ang lalaking dating tumalo kay Goliath… ngayon hindi na kayang painitin ng kumot.
At kapag humihina ang isang lider… maraming taong nagsisimulang magplano.
Dito papasok si Adonijah.
Sabi ng Biblia:
“Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king.” (1 Kings 1:5)
Napakabigat ng verse na iyon.
Pansinin:
Hindi sinabi ng Biblia na:
“Tinawag siya ng Diyos.” “Pinili siya ng Diyos.” “Pinahiran siya ng Diyos.”
Ang sabi:
“Exalted himself.”
Sa Hebrew:
וַיִּתְנַשֵּׂא אֲדֹנִיָּה
“Vayyitnasse Adoniyah”
Ibig sabihin: Itinaas niya ang sarili niya.
Sariling promote. Sariling coronation. Sariling agenda.
Nakakatakot isipin… dahil buhay pa rin ang spirit na iyon hanggang ngayon.
Maraming tao ang gustong mauna sa timing ng Diyos.
Gusto agad ng platform. Gusto agad ng title. Gusto agad ng influence.
Pero ayaw dumaan sa proseso.
Ayaw maghintay.
Ayaw masaktan.
Ayaw madurog.
Kaya marami ang gumagawa ng sariling trono.
At iyon mismo ang ginawa ni Adonijah.
Ang mas nakakatakot?
Mukha naman talaga siyang qualified.
Gwapo. Anak ni David. May royal blood. May connections. May supporters.
Sabi pa ng Biblia:
“He also was a very goodly man.” (1 Kings 1:6)
Sa Hebrew:
טוֹב תֹּאַר מְאֹד
“Tov to’ar me’od”
Napakagandang anyo.
At dito madalas nadadaya ang tao.
Akala natin kapag magaling magsalita… anointed na. Kapag charismatic… chosen na. Kapag sikat… approved na ng Diyos.
Pero hindi kailanman naloko ang Diyos sa appearance.
Nakita na natin ito noon kay Saul.
Mukhang hari. Pero hindi surrendered.
At ito ang masakit na realidad:
May mga taong mukhang tama externally… pero hindi pala sila ang pinili ng Diyos.
Nagtipon si Adonijah ng mga chariots. Mga kabayo. Limampung lalaking tatakbo sa harapan niya.
Parang campaign rally.
Gusto niyang makita ng mga tao:
“Ito na ang susunod na hari.”
Pero hindi kayang gumawa ng tunay na calling ang applause.
Hindi kayang palitan ng popularity ang anointing.
At pagkatapos… may isang verse na sobrang tumatagos lalo na sa mga magulang.
“His father had not displeased him at any time...” (1 Kings 1:6)
Hindi siya kinorek ni David.
Hindi siya sinaway. Hindi siya nilimitahan. Hindi siya dinisiplina.
Nakakatindig-balahibo iyon.
Dahil minsan, ang love na walang correction… nagiging destruction.
Lumaki si Adonijah na walang restraint.
At kapag hindi natutong magpasakop ang pride… gusto nitong umupo sa trono.
Maraming tao ngayon ang gusto ng authority pero galit sa correction.
Kapag na-rebuke, umaalis. Kapag na-call out, nagtatampo. Kapag may accountability, biglang nawawala.
Pero ang hindi kino-correct na pride… nakamamatay spiritually.
Pagkatapos nito, nagsimulang kumuha ng allies si Adonijah.
Sumama si Joab. Sumama si Abiathar na pari.
At ito ang delikado sa rebellion.
Minsan supported pa ito ng mga respected na tao.
Kaya maraming believers ang nalilito:
“Paano nangyari iyon? Spiritual naman sila.”
Pero tandaan ito:
Hindi lahat ng nasa paligid ng holy things… surrendered kay God.
Kahit pari puwedeng maging compromised. Kahit experienced leaders puwedeng malinlang ng momentum.
Pagkatapos, gumawa si Adonijah ng sacrificial feast.
Pansinin mo.
Binalot niya sa religious appearance ang rebellion.
At ginagawa pa rin iyan hanggang ngayon.
May mga taong gumagamit ng “God told me” para takpan ang sariling ambition.
Pero hindi lahat ng mukhang spiritual… galing sa Diyos.
At pagkatapos… may isang detail na sobrang revealing.
Hindi niya inimbitahan si Solomon.
Alam niya kasi.
Deep inside, alam niyang may totoong pinili ang Diyos.
At madalas, alam ng flesh kung sino ang tunay na threat.
Ayaw ni Adonijah kay Solomon dahil si Solomon ang covenant choice.
At dito pumapasok si Bathsheba.
Ang babaeng madalas maalala lang dahil sa scandal.
Pero dito… ginamit siya ng Diyos para protektahan ang linya na hahantong kay Jesucristo.
Lumapit si Nathan na propeta.
At napakaganda nito.
Habang may taong nagtataas sa sarili… gumagalaw ang Diyos sa pamamagitan ng prophetic truth.
Sinabi ni Nathan:
“Hast thou not heard that Adonijah... doth reign, and David our lord knoweth it not?” (1 Kings 1:11)
Inaagaw na ang kaharian habang buhay pa ang hari.
At spiritually… nangyayari rin ito.
Habang tulog ang discernment ng tao… may ibang bagay nang umuupo sa puso.
Pride. Lust. Bitterness. Addiction. Control. Ego. Self-worship.
Unti-unti silang nagiging hari sa buhay ng tao.
Hanggang sa maalala ni Bathsheba si David tungkol sa pangako kay Solomon.
Kinumpirma ni Nathan.
At biglang nagbago ang atmosphere.
Tumayo si David.
Mahina ang katawan. Pero buhay pa rin ang covenant.
Napakalalim nito.
Dahil kahit maraming failure si David… hindi tumigil ang plano ng Diyos.
Pinili na ni God si Solomon.
Hindi dahil perfect siya. Hindi dahil malinis ang story nila Bathsheba.
Kundi dahil ang plano ng Diyos ay nakatayo sa grace.
Iniutos ni David:
“Cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule.” (1 Kings 1:33)
Ang mule ng hari ay simbolo ng authority.
Pagkatapos, pinahiran si Solomon nina Zadok at Nathan.
At sumigaw ang bayan:
“God save king Solomon.”
Sa Hebrew:
יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹה
“Yechi hamelech Shelomoh”
“Mabuhay si Haring Solomon.”
At narinig iyon ni Adonijah.
Isipin mo ang pakiramdam.
Akala niya siya na.
Akala niya secured na.
Akala niya sapat na ang support.
Pero sa isang iglap… nalantad na hindi siya ang pinili.
Ito ang mahirap tanggapin minsan:
Hindi lahat ng open door ay galing sa Diyos. Hindi lahat ng opportunity ay destiny. Hindi lahat ng applause ay confirmation.
Minsan hinahayaan ng Diyos na lumabas ang tunay na laman ng puso bago dumating ang judgment.
Tumakbo si Adonijah sa altar at hinawakan ang horns nito para humingi ng mercy.
At dito sobrang ganda ng puso ni Solomon.
Nagpakita siya ng mercy.
Pero hindi talaga nagbago si Adonijah.
Kalaunan, sinubukan ulit niyang kumuha ng kapangyarihan sa pamamagitan ni Abishag.
Sa culture noon, ang pagkuha sa dating concubine ng hari ay parang pag-angkin din sa trono.
Naintindihan agad iyon ni Solomon.
Hindi pa rin pala sumusuko si Adonijah.
Natakot lang siya.
At may malaking difference ang takot at tunay na repentance.
Maraming tao ang tumitigil lang pansamantala dahil takot sa consequence.
Pero hindi pa talaga surrendered kay God.
Ang kwentong ito ay hindi lang tungkol sa politics.
Tungkol ito sa puso ng tao.
Sa desire nating kontrolin ang hindi naman atin.
Sa tendency nating pilitin ang hindi pa ibinibigay ng Diyos.
Sa pride na gustong maupo sa trono.
At dito lalong lumalalim ang Gospel.
Dahil si Jesus ang kabaligtaran ni Adonijah.
Si Adonijah: Itinaas ang sarili.
Si Jesus: Nagpakumbaba.
Sa Filipos 2, sinabi sa Greek:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
“Heauton ekenosen”
“He emptied Himself.”
Si Adonijah gustong kumuha ng trono.
Si Jesus pumunta sa krus.
Si Adonijah gumamit ng image.
Si Jesus “despised and rejected of men.”
Si Adonijah naghahanap ng supporters.
Si Jesus naghugas ng paa.
At iyon ang tunay na Hari.
Hindi lang dumating si Cristo para ilantad ang maling hari sa puso mo.
Dumating Siya para palitan iyon.
Baka pagod ka na.
Pagod na kakapilit. Pagod na kakacontrol. Pagod na kakahabol ng approval. Pagod na kakabuhat ng identity na hindi naman galing sa Diyos.
Pero may freedom sa surrender.
Dahil ang tunay na itinatalaga ng Diyos… hindi kailangang pilitin ng laman para manatili.
O simpleng: “Jesus, Ikaw na lang.”
Maging totoo tayo.
Mas malalim ito kaysa inaakala ng iba.
At kung may kilala kang pilit kinokontrol ang lahat… share mo ito sa kanila.
Baka may taong tahimik nang napapagod kakahawak sa trono na hindi naman talaga kanila.
Dahil darating ang araw na kakailanganin mong maalala ang difference ng opportunity at divine appointment.
May mga taong nawawala ang kaluluwa habang hinahabol ang koronang hindi naman sila tinawag na isuot.
